headline: The yen tore 1.3% higher in the Tokyo morning, Japanese equities took the entire hit - Nikkei 225 down 1130.51 points, or 1.70%, to close at 65269.33, and it closed AT the session low - and almost none of it travelled. S&P futures are down 0.14% and Nasdaq futures down 0.15% against the last print before CME's Labor Day halt. AUD/JPY, the carry barometer, is flat. This is a Japan-specific rate shock, not a global carry unwind, and the distinction is the whole trade. Meanwhile crude went up for a fourth day - WTI 93.98, Brent 98.65 - after a drone strike on Saudi Aramco's 400kb/d Jizan refinery, its third hit in two months. US cash markets reopen at 9:30 having not traded since Friday, with Canadian counter-tariffs live since 12:01 AM and China's August trade data already on the tape.
client_frame_short: Three days of news are about to hit a market that has not been open to absorb any of it. The honest framing for a client this morning is that **the scariest-looking number overnight - Japan down 1.7% - is the one least likely to matter to a US portfolio**, because it was caused by a Japanese interest-rate story and the instruments that would carry it abroad did not move. What deserves attention instead is quieter and more durable: three central banks on three continents are now expected to raise rates, and gasoline and diesel are grinding higher on a physical supply story that no monetary policy can fix. Those are the things that show up in a client's life and in a bond allocation.
client_frame:
The temptation this morning is to lead with Japan, because down 1.7% is the biggest number on the page. Resist it. Tokyo fell because the yen appreciated 1.3% - from about 155.5 late Monday to a 152.88 low - and a stronger yen mechanically compresses the earnings of the exporters that dominate the index. Transportation equipment fell 4.04% and JTEKT fell 8.68%. That is a currency-translation story about Japanese companies, and it is entirely rational for Japanese equities to fall on it. The question a client actually needs answered is whether it says anything about their own portfolio, and the evidence this morning says no. If a yen surge were unwinding global carry trades, AUD/JPY would be sliding and US futures would be following; AUD/JPY is down 0.05% and US futures are down about a seventh of a percent. We tested the link directly rather than asserting it: across the overnight window the correlation between hourly USD/JPY moves and hourly Nasdaq futures moves was minus 0.11, effectively nothing, and the two markets did not even bottom together - the yen hit its extreme six hours before Nasdaq futures hit theirs, and futures actually RALLIED while the yen was strongest. The contagion story is available, quotable, and wrong.

What is worth a client's attention is the thing no one is putting in a headline: the world's central banks have quietly reversed direction, all at once. Futures now price a 57% chance the Federal Reserve HIKES next week and assign zero probability to a cut at any meeting through March. The ECB meets Thursday, having already raised rates in June. The Bank of Japan meets the following week. Australia's market has moved from under 10% odds of a hike a month ago to 67% now. For a decade the reflex answer to any equity wobble was that the central bank would come to the rescue; that put has been sold. It does not mean sell equities - it means the diversifier that worked from 2009 to 2021 is not the diversifier that works now, and a client whose bond allocation is built for rate cuts owns the wrong bonds.

The second durable story is at the pump, and it is the one clients will raise unprompted. Diesel's national average is 5.9012 dollars a gallon, three hundredths of a cent below the all-time record it set YESTERDAY, and it is up 2.20 dollars in a year. Regular is 4.1514, up 95 cents year-over-year but still 17% below its own 2022 record. Diesel is the freight input, so it propagates into goods prices with a lag of months, and it is rising because of physical supply disruption - a fourth straight up day in crude, the Jizan refinery struck for the third time in two months, Hormuz transits running at roughly 10 vessels a day against about 125 before the war. That is a genuine inflation impulse arriving from the supply side into a Fed that is already leaning toward hiking, which is precisely the combination that makes the coming CPI print on Friday matter more than usual. Note carefully that we have no verified consensus estimate for either Thursday's PPI or Friday's CPI - none was published by any primary wire we could reach - so anyone quoting a forecast to you this week is quoting a vendor's model, not a poll.

The practical counsel is unchanged and worth saying plainly: today's open will look noisy because it is absorbing three days of accumulated news in one print, and noise at an open after a long weekend is not information. The two things actually worth repositioning around are the rate-hiking regime and the supply-side energy impulse, and neither of them requires acting before lunch.
geo_headlines: JAPAN - THE ONLY MARKET THAT ACTUALLY MOVED, AND IT CLOSED ON ITS LOW. The Nikkei 225 fell 1130.51 points, or 1.70%, to 65269.33, and the Topix fell 1.83% to 4050.33. Two independent wires carry all three figures identically, and a third source - the quote vendor's own index feed - returns 65269.33, minus 1130.51, minus 1.70% against a prior close of 66399.84, with a session high of 66791.84 and a session LOW equal to the close. Closing at the low of the day after a 1522-point range is a capitulation pattern, not an orderly repricing. The cause is the currency: USD/JPY went from 155.54 at 17:00 Monday Tokyo time to 153.77 by 10:00 Tuesday, with our own tick data showing a 152.881 low, the strongest yen since roughly late February. Tokyo Prime breadth was 362 advancers against 1158 decliners, and the damage was concentrated exactly where a currency story predicts: transportation equipment minus 4.04%, precision instruments minus 3.64%, electric appliances minus 2.76%, with JTEKT minus 8.68%, its worst day since August 2024. The breadth and sector figures come from an aggregator rather than an exchange feed and are flagged as single-sourced, though its index close matches the wires exactly. SoftBank Group was the conspicuous exception, up 5.45%.

THE CONTAGION TRADE, TESTED AND FALSIFIED. The available narrative this morning is that a yen surge unwound carry trades and dragged US futures lower. We tested it rather than repeating it, and it does not survive. Across the overnight window the correlation between hourly USD/JPY changes and hourly Nasdaq futures changes was minus 0.112 over twelve observations - indistinguishable from zero. The timing is worse for the story than the correlation: USD/JPY bottomed at 152.881 between 02:00 and 03:00 UTC, while Nasdaq futures bottomed at 29481.75 at 08:00 UTC, six hours later. In the window when the yen was at its strongest, from 00:00 to 04:00 UTC, Nasdaq futures RALLIED 0.37%. They only fell later, from 04:00 to 08:00 UTC, while the yen was WEAKENING. And the instrument that exists to express carry unwind, AUD/JPY, is down 0.05%. The correct reading is that Japanese equities are genuinely yen-sensitive - that link is real and well documented - and US equity futures, in this window, were not. Report the two moves; do not connect them.

OIL - FOURTH UP DAY, AND A PHYSICAL HIT ON SAUDI REFINING. WTI is 93.98 and Brent 98.65, with Brent having set a six-week high on Monday and now up a third consecutive session. The new development in the window is physical: Saudi Aramco's Jizan refinery, 400000 barrels a day of capacity, was struck by a drone on Monday 9/7 - the third hit on that facility in two months - with the Houthis claiming the attack. Two wires carry it. No barrels-lost figure has been published and the exact hour is unverified, which is why this is flagged escalation-worthy rather than priced. Context that makes it matter: Hormuz commodity transits are running a ten-day average near 10 vessels a day, the lowest since May, against roughly 125 large commercial vessels a day before the war began on 28 February. Two caveats a desk should carry - the pre-war baseline itself is disputed, with one wire saying 125 a day and another saying 100, and Kpler and S&P Global publish materially different Hormuz counts, so any transit number must travel with its vendor's name attached.

THE OVER-REPORTED NON-STORY: IRAN'S HORMUZ EXCLUSION ZONE. Several outlets are writing as though Iran has declared a new restricted maritime zone in the Gulf. It has not, as far as any source dated inside our window shows. What actually happened is that Mohsen Rezaei TRAILED such a zone on Sunday 9/6 as coming in coming days. Announced is not declared, and declared is not enforced. We searched specifically for an in-window declaration and found none. The same discipline flagged a second trap: multiple wires printed intraday Asian levels as if they were closes. One agency ran the Nikkei at 66170.34 and down 0.3% and the Kospi at 7060.79 and up 1.0%; both indices closed materially lower, the Nikkei about 901 points below that print and the Kospi below 7000 after trading above 7060. One vendor published both a Kospi surges past 7000 piece and a Kospi drops below 7000 piece on the same day. Resolve by timestamp, not by preference.

CENTRAL BANKS ARE HIKING ON THREE CONTINENTS AT ONCE, AND THIS IS THE REAL STORY. CME's FedWatch cohort assigns a 57.4% probability to a 25bp HIKE at next week's FOMC and a 42.6% probability to a hold, with the cumulative probability of at least one hike rising to 68.7% by October, 84.7% by December and 92.8% by March. The probability of a CUT at any meeting through March 2027 is exactly zero. The ECB decides Thursday, and it is worth being precise about the starting point because it is routinely misdescribed: the current 2.25% deposit rate is the result of a 25bp HIKE on 11 June 2026, held on 23 July - this is not a cutting cycle being interrupted, it is a hiking cycle already underway. The Bank of Japan meets 17-18 September and will not say what time it will announce. And Australian swaps now imply a 67% chance of a September RBA hike against under 10% a month ago, which is the single largest repricing anywhere in the window. A client whose bond portfolio is positioned for the 2010s policy reaction function is positioned for the wrong decade.

DIESEL SET AN ALL-TIME RECORD YESTERDAY AND IS THREE HUNDREDTHS OF A CENT BELOW IT TODAY. AAA's national average for diesel is 5.9012 dollars a gallon against the all-time high of 5.9015 set on 9/7/26 - so today is NOT a record, by 0.0003 dollars, and that distinction is made deliberately because the honest version of this fact is more useful than the dramatic one. Diesel is up 0.2687 in a week, 0.5836 in a month and 2.1991 in a year, a 59% annual increase. Regular gasoline is 4.1514, up 0.0009 on the day and 0.9516 on the year, and remains about 17% below its own record of 5.0165 from June 2022 - so this is emphatically not a generalised fuel spike, it is a distillate squeeze. That asymmetry is diagnostic: distillate is the freight and industrial input, so it feeds goods disinflation into reversal with a lag, and it is the fuel most exposed to refinery outages of exactly the kind Jizan just suffered. Premium was unchanged on the day and diesel ticked DOWN day-over-day, so the prints are mixed, not uniformly higher.

CHINA'S AUGUST TRADE DATA PUBLISHED, AND THE IMPORT NUMBER MISSED. Exports rose 25.0% year-over-year against a Reuters poll of 35 economists looking for exactly 25.0%, so exports were in line. Imports rose 28.2% against a 30.0% consensus - a genuine MISS, and the more informative of the two numbers, because import strength had been the rebalancing story for six consecutive months. The trade surplus came in at 119.09 billion dollars against a 119.05 billion poll and 112.5 billion in July, so marginally above. Total trade was 683.8 billion, up 26.3%, and cumulative trade for the first eight months of 2026 is up 17.6%. SOURCING CAVEAT, stated because it matters: we did not obtain the GACC primary release itself. Every figure here is wire-derived, and two outlets citing the same customs release is not independent corroboration - though three separate wire lineages quote the export figure with identical decimals, which partially satisfies the quoted-row test. Treat as REPORTED rather than primary.

CANADA'S COUNTER-TARIFFS ARE LIVE AS OF 12:01 AM ET THIS MORNING. Finance Canada's own published list confirms roughly 27.6 billion Canadian dollars of US-origin goods now carry 15, 25 and 50% duties, each matching the corresponding US rate good-for-good, across more than 600 product classifications spanning steel and aluminium, dairy, pulp and paper, appliances, electronics and agricultural equipment. Goods in transit on the day of coming-into-force are exempt. We looked specifically for a last-minute delay, carve-out or ministerial reprieve and found none dated in window; as of late Monday afternoon Canadian officials said no further talks with US negotiators were scheduled. ONE ARITHMETIC TRAP TO DISARM BEFORE A DESK TRIPS ON IT: coverage variously cites 20 billion US dollars, 27.6 billion Canadian dollars and 28 billion. These are ONE programme quoted in two currencies with one rounding, not two or three separate programmes. Today's US open is the first session to price any of it.

RUSSIA STRUCK KYIV WITH BALLISTIC MISSILES HOURS AFTER THE US ENVOYS LEFT, AND THE CASUALTY COUNT DOES NOT RECONCILE. The strikes came within hours of Witkoff and Kushner departing, and Poland scrambled air defence in response. The casualty reporting is genuinely UNRECONCILED across three outlets - six injured, two killed, and four killed - and we are reporting the disagreement rather than picking the middle or the highest number, because in the first hours after a strike the spread between sources is information about reporting conditions, not about the event. The market-relevant point is not the casualty count but the sequencing: a strike timed to the departure of American negotiators is a deliberate signal about the negotiation, and it is the kind of convex, cheap-to-underweight risk that gets ignored until it is not. Paired with the Jizan refinery strike, the window contained two separate physical escalations against energy and civilian infrastructure.

WHAT DID NOT HAPPEN, WHICH IS ALSO REPORTABLE, AND WHAT WE COULD NOT GET. Verified NON-developments in the window: no CENTCOM press release dated 9/6, 9/7 or 9/8 - the most recent item on the official index remains 5 September; no presidential statement on the Federal Reserve inside the window, because the LOWER THE RATE post everyone is quoting is from FRIDAY and is out of window; no Fed commentary of any kind, because the blackout has run since 12:00 AM ET Saturday 5 September and runs to 11:59 PM Thursday 17 September; no new ECB sources story; no Bank of Japan or Ministry of Finance official comment on the yen despite a 1.3% move; and no US-listed guidance change, M&A or earnings release. HONEST GAPS, disclosed because absence of a sourced answer is itself reportable: we could not obtain a Japanese 10-year JGB level for Tuesday, could not isolate an in-window war-risk premium, could not date any Hormuz transit count to 9/7 or 9/8 specifically, and found the UK 10-year gilt quoted at 5.1345% as-of 9/6 against an undated 5.1802%, which we leave UNRECONCILED rather than averaging.
